repos.title: REMORY: Learning Residual Memory for Context Compaction
repos.paper_summary: Remory is a learned memory network that adds a bounded set of continuous soft tokens after a textual compaction summary, so a frozen LLM can approximate its continuation with the full history. The network is conditioned on the summary and emits 64 tokens per block of up to 1,024 source positions, capped at 4,096 slots. Training has two stages: reconstruction of source passages, then summary-conditioned continuation, using reverse KL against a teacher that sees the full history. On SummHay (92 queries, Qwen3.8-27B), summary plus memory raises citation F1 from 56.98 to 61.03 and joint score from 39.84 to 43.39, with coverage nearly unchanged (67.55 to 67.95), using 5.2% of raw-context positions. Within-actor agent runs improve: Qwen AutomationBench rises from 35.5 to 45.3, Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 71.9 to 76.4, and BrowseComp from 74.0 to 77.0. Limitations: the 95% bootstrap interval for the SummHay joint-score gain is [+0.74, +6.21]; Terminal-Bench and BrowseComp use one run per configuration; cost estimates exclude memory-network execution; and the first-action preference judgments do not measure outcomes.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Summaries alone may miss context needed later, so Remory adds learned memory tokens after a summary.

digest_headlines.heading: Residual Memory
digest_headlines.headline: A memory network trains soft tokens so a frozen actor matches its full-history continuation.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Residual memory raises SummHay joint score and agent scores while reducing repeated tool outputs and errors.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Remory extends summary-plus-retrieval memory with a continuous representation learned from the checkpoint.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Attribution, agent scores, and preferred next actions support the residual formulation as a bounded supplement.

repos.title: RAG-Anything: All-in-One RAG Framework
repos.paper_summary: RAG-Anything is a unified multimodal retrieval-augmented generation framework that builds a dual graph over documents: a cross-modal graph anchored on non-text units (figures, tables, equations) and a text-based graph, merged by entity-name alignment. Retrieval combines graph neighborhood expansion with dense embedding search over entities, relations, and chunks, and a VLM answers using text context plus the dereferenced visual content. On DocBench, it reaches 63.4% overall accuracy versus 61.0% for MMGraphRAG, 58.4% for LightRAG, and 51.2% for GPT-4o-mini. On MMLongBench, it reaches 42.8% versus 38.9% for LightRAG and 37.7% for MMGraphRAG. The gap grows with document length: on DocBench it is over 13 points for documents over 100 pages. Ablations on DocBench show 60.0% for chunk-only retrieval and 62.4% without the reranker, against 63.4% for the full system. All baselines use GPT-4o-mini, and accuracy is judged by GPT-4o-mini. The paper reports no variance across runs. Evaluation covers two benchmarks only.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing RAG systems handle only text, so multimodal documents are poorly served; the paper proposes RAG-Anything to fix this.

digest_headlines.heading: The RAG-Anything Framework
digest_headlines.headline: RAG-Anything decomposes documents into typed units, builds two linked graphs, and retrieves through both structure and embeddings.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: On MMLongBench, RAG-Anything scores 42.8% overall versus 37.7% for MMGraphRAG, with gains growing on longer documents.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work groups graph-enhanced RAG and multimodal RAG, and argues that prior multimodal systems fragment by modality.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The paper concludes that dual-graph retrieval helps long documents and identifies text-centric bias and rigid spatial processing as failure modes.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists dataset statistics, extra case studies, the three multimodal prompts, the accuracy prompt, and failure-case analyses.

repos.title: Deep Photo Style Transfer
repos.paper_summary: The paper introduces a deep-learning method for photographic style transfer that preserves the photorealism of the input image while accurately matching the color and texture of a reference style image. The approach extends the Neural Style algorithm by adding two constraints to the optimization objective. First, a photorealism regularization term ensures the transformation from input to output is locally affine in color space, preventing spatial distortions like wiggly edges. This term uses the Matting Laplacian matrix derived from the input image. Second, an augmented style loss incorporates semantic segmentation masks for both images, restricting style transfer between semantically equivalent regions (e.g., sky to sky) to prevent "spillover" artifacts. The method uses a pre-trained VGG-19 network, with content features from `conv4_2` and style features from layers `conv1_1` through `conv5_1`. Optimization runs in 3–5 minutes on an NVIDIA Titan X GPU. In user studies, the method produced photorealistic results comparable to global histogram transfer methods, but achieved higher style faithfulness than Reinhard et al., Pitié et al., and Photoshop Match Color in over 80% of comparisons. Limitations include failure cases under extreme semantic mismatch between input and reference, which require manual segmentation masks to resolve.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Photographic style transfer must avoid painting-like distortion while keeping the reference style faithful.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: The method adds a locally affine color regularizer and semantic segmentation masks to Neural Style optimization.

digest_headlines.heading: Implementation Details
digest_headlines.headline: The implementation uses a pretrained convolutional network, two-stage optimization and merged segmentation classes.

digest_headlines.heading: Results and Comparison
digest_headlines.headline: Compared with Neural Style, patch-based and global transfer methods, the approach avoids distortion and was judged most faithful more than 80% of the time.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: The approach transfers reference style faithfully across time of day, weather, season and artistic edits while keeping outputs photorealistic.

repos.title: ASPIRE: Agentic /Skills Discovery for Robotics
repos.paper_summary: ASPIRE is a continual learning system in which a coding agent (Claude Opus 4.6) writes and repairs robot control programs in the CaP-X code-as-policy framework, distilling validated fixes into a reusable skill library and using evolutionary search over candidate programs. A closed-loop execution engine records per-primitive multimodal traces, such as perception overlays and motion-planning returns, which let the agent localize failures and validate repairs. On LIBERO-Pro, Robosuite, and BEHAVIOR-1K, Aspire outperforms CaP-Agent0 and VLA baselines (OpenVLA, π0, π0.5). Reported gains include up to 77 points on LIBERO-Pro perturbation suites, bimanual handover improving from 20% to 92%, and navigate-and-pick-up-radio improving from 56% to 88%. Skills learned on LIBERO-90 transfer zero-shot to LIBERO-Pro Long, reaching 23% (position) and 38% (task) success. Limitations: the system depends on one frozen frontier LLM, the action API is fixed, the skill library lacks pruning, and the search is compute-intensive.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: ASPIRE lets a coding agent write and repair robot programs from fine-grained traces and reuse validated fixes across tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: A coordinator dispatches actor agents whose validated repairs are admitted to a shared skill library after verifier checks.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: ASPIRE beats prior coding agents and end-to-end policies on three benchmarks, rising from 20% to 92% on bimanual handover.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work spans end-to-end robot policies, executable robot programs, and skill libraries, where ASPIRE stores attributed repair knowledge.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Stated limits include dependence on a frozen language model, a fixed robot interface, one-time skill checks, and manual real-world resets.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: ASPIRE pairs execution traces and evolutionary search with a growing skill library, reaching 99% average success on LIBERO-Pro with Claude Opus 5.5.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists skill-library entries, benchmark tables, zero-shot and per-task results, the real-robot harness, and case-study details.

repos.title: Scaling in Games: Continued Pre-Training For Embodied Agents In Diverse Virtual Worlds
repos.paper_summary: Scaling in Games (Zhang, Chen, Yang et al.) is a controlled study of continued pre-training (CPT) for embodied game agents that vary data volume, data diversity, and model size. The authors train 120 configurations spanning 0.8B to 27B parameters, 50 to 1,600 hours of gameplay, and five mixtures from Minecraft-only to multi-game. Models take screen frames and output keyboard-mouse actions. Evaluation covers in-corpus worlds (Minecraft, Doom), related worlds (OmniGameArena), and distant worlds (GameWorld), using validation losses and benchmark scores. Diversity improves related-world transfer, while distant-world gains stay limited. Larger models use data more efficiently but generalize worse under single-game training. A three-factor scaling law fits training, Minecraft, and in-corpus losses with R² of 0.980, 0.982, and 0.995. On MCU, the 27B-S1 model reaches 63.3% average success, and under real-time evaluation the 9B-S3 model scores 25.3 versus 19.2 for the best frontier model tested. The limits are that training is behavior cloning without task feedback, and the distant-world gap persists.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Virtual worlds vary in visuals, physics, controls and goals, so the study asks whether heterogeneous gameplay data helps or interferes.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier virtual-agent work used single-environment specialists or foundation models, and none isolated data, diversity and model size together.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries and Experiment Framework
digest_headlines.headline: The study frames gameplay as reason-then-act steps and trains a 120-configuration grid over model size, data budget and mixture.

digest_headlines.heading: Scaling and Generalization in Heterogeneous Virtual Worlds
digest_headlines.headline: More data and diversity improve in-corpus and related-world results, but gains in distant worlds stay limited.

digest_headlines.heading: Comparing with Frontier Models
digest_headlines.headline: Models are competitive with Minecraft specialists and frontier models in 3D worlds and lead frontier models in real-time play.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Gains in related worlds do not reliably reach distant worlds, and the imitation objective may help explain the gap.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics Statement
digest_headlines.headline: Training uses publicly released gameplay datasets under their licenses, and the authors collect no new recordings or personal data.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers mixture accounting, the out-of-distribution validation set, sparse reasoning annotations and comparisons with related scaling studies.

repos.title: LlamaFactory: Unified Efficient Fine-Tuning of 100+ Language Models
repos.paper_summary:
LlamaFactory is a unified framework integrating efficient fine-tuning methods to adapt over 100 large language models without custom code. It comprises three modules: a Model Loader attaching adapters like LoRA, QLoRA, and GaLore; a Data Worker standardizing dataset formats; and a Trainer supporting pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, and DPO. A key feature is model-sharing RLHF, which uses dynamic adapter switching to run the full pipeline on a single pre-trained model. The web interface LlamaBoard allows users to configure experiments and monitor training in real time.

The authors validate the framework on an NVIDIA A100 GPU using Gemma-2B, Llama2-7B, and Llama2-13B. On a corpus of roughly 400K tokens from PubMed abstracts, 4-bit QLoRA reduces peak memory to 5.21 GB for Gemma-2B compared to 17.06 GB for full tuning, while LoRA achieves a throughput of 3521 tokens/s. In downstream text generation tasks with 2,000 training examples, LoRA and QLoRA generally match or exceed full-tuning ROUGE scores across eight instruction-tuned models. Limitations include the requirement for adapter-based methods when using quantized weights and the fact that full-tuning Llama2-13B exceeds the 40GB memory limit of the test hardware.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Fine-tuning large language models is costly, so LlamaFactory unifies efficient fine-tuning methods in one framework.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing fine-tuning frameworks support fewer efficient methods than LlamaFactory, as its feature comparison shows.

digest_headlines.heading: Efficient Fine-Tuning Techniques
digest_headlines.headline: The paper groups efficient fine-tuning into optimization methods, such as LoRA, and computation methods, such as flash attention.

digest_headlines.heading: LlamaFactory Framework
digest_headlines.headline: LlamaFactory has three modules, Model Loader, Data Worker and Trainer, with a web interface called LlamaBoard.

digest_headlines.heading: Empirical Study
digest_headlines.headline: Across tested models, quantized low-rank adaptation used the least memory and low-rank adaptation scored best on most generation tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Future work targets more modalities, parallel training strategies and stronger methods for conversational models.

digest_headlines.heading: Broader Impact and Responsible Use
digest_headlines.headline: The authors expect the framework to benefit open-source communities, and require users to follow model licenses.

repos.title: LightRAG: Simple and Fast Retrieval-Augmented Generation
repos.paper_summary:
LightRAG is a graph-based retrieval-augmented generation system. An LLM extracts entities and relations from chunks of size 1200, profiles each as a key-value pair, and deduplicates the resulting graph. At query time, local keywords match entities and global keywords match relations, and one-hop neighbors of the matches are added as context for a general LLM. New documents are indexed by merging their subgraphs into the existing graph instead of rebuilding it.

The evaluation uses four UltraDomain datasets (Agriculture, CS, Legal, Mix), with 125 generated questions per dataset, GPT-4o-mini as the default LLM, and pairwise LLM judgments reported as win rates. Against NaiveRAG on Legal, LightRAG wins 84.8% overall. Against GraphRAG, the margins are small: overall win rates of 54.8% on Agriculture, 52.0% on CS, 52.8% on Legal, and 49.6% on Mix.

The judgments come from a single LLM judge, not human or ground-truth labels. The ablation and cost results are cut off in the provided text, so this summary does not report them.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing RAG systems rely on flat representations and produce fragmented answers, so the paper proposes graph-based indexing with incremental updates.

digest_headlines.heading: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
digest_headlines.headline: The paper formalizes RAG as indexing and retrieval followed by generation, and sets three design goals for an efficient system.

digest_headlines.heading: The LightRAG Architecture
digest_headlines.headline: LightRAG builds a knowledge graph with LLM extraction, updates it incrementally, and retrieves through dual-level keyword matching.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: LightRAG wins LLM-judged comparisons against four baselines on UltraDomain datasets, and uses far fewer retrieval tokens than GraphRAG.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work finds graph-based RAG lacks dynamic updates, and surveys three ways LLMs are combined with graph data.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: LightRAG is concluded to improve retrieval speed and quality and cut LLM inference costs through graph indexing and incremental updates.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists dataset statistics, a case study against NaiveRAG, and the prompts for graph generation, query generation, keyword extraction and evaluation.

repos.title: Plan-and-Solve Prompting: Improving Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Reasoning by Large Language Models
repos.paper_summary: Plan-and-Solve (PS) Prompting is a zero-shot prompting strategy for large language models that instructs the model to devise a plan dividing a task into subtasks before executing them. The extended variant, PS+, adds instructions to extract relevant variables and calculate intermediate results. On ten datasets covering arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning using GPT-3 (text-davinci-003), PS+ outperforms Zero-shot-CoT by an average of 6.3% on arithmetic tasks, reaching 76.7% accuracy compared to 70.4%. It also exceeds Zero-shot-Program-of-Thought on five of six arithmetic benchmarks. Error analysis on GSM8K shows PS+ reduces calculation errors from 7% to 5% and missing-step errors from 12% to 7%, though semantic misunderstanding errors remain at 27%. The paper notes two limitations: prompt sensitivity requires careful manual design, and the method does not address semantic understanding errors.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Zero-shot chain-of-thought errors are split into calculation, missing-step, and semantic errors, and a plan-based prompt targets two of them.

digest_headlines.heading: Plan-and-Solve Prompting
digest_headlines.headline: Plan-and-Solve prompting uses a zero-shot trigger that asks the model to devise and carry out a plan, followed by an answer-extraction prompt.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments use ten benchmarks with text-davinci-003 and compare against zero-shot and few-shot baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Results
digest_headlines.headline: PS+ outperforms Zero-shot-CoT on all arithmetic datasets and averages 76.7 against 77.6 for Manual-CoT.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work places Plan-and-Solve among chain-of-thought methods that use zero-shot prompting and planning.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude that plan-based zero-shot prompting outperforms Zero-shot-CoT and matches few-shot CoT on some arithmetic datasets.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Prompt design is labour-intensive and the method does not address semantic misunderstanding errors.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics
digest_headlines.headline: The paper lists the datasets and their licences and states that the prompts contain no personal information or discriminatory wording.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists trigger-sentence ablations for every dataset and example outputs from Zero-shot-PS+.

repos.title: Interpretable Machine Learning for Science with PySR and SymbolicRegression.jl
repos.paper_summary: PySR is an open-source library for symbolic regression that discovers interpretable mathematical expressions from data. The method uses a multi-population evolutionary algorithm with tournament selection, simulated annealing, and an evolve-simplify-optimize loop to optimize real constants within discovered expressions. The backend, `SymbolicRegression.jl`, uses Julia’s just-in-time compilation to fuse user-defined operators into SIMD kernels at runtime, enabling distributed computation across clusters. PySR introduces “EmpiricalBench,” a benchmark measuring the recovery of historical empirical equations from original and synthetic datasets. In this evaluation, PySR outperforms deep learning-based approaches EQL and SR-Transformer in discovering these equations, while remaining competitive with other evolutionary methods like Operon and DSR. Limitations include the lack of native GPU support and the requirement for users to define custom operators in both Julia and SymPy for full export functionality.

repos.title: Latent Sparse Attention: Towards Subquadratic Ultra-Long Context Attention
repos.paper_summary:
Latent Sparse Attention (LSA) is a sparse attention layer for ultra-long context. It clusters keys in a learned latent space, and each query scores cluster centroids instead of every key. Keys are pooled four to one, grouped into buckets by Ward's agglomerative clustering, and queries pick top buckets (flat search) or descend a tree with beam search (Tree, which is subquadratic in prefill). Attention then runs over sink, window, and selected keys. Distilled-LSA (D-LSA) adds LSA to a frozen pre-trained model by training only small per-layer projections and a temperature against the frozen layer's attention. Native-LSA (N-LSA) is trained on next-token loss alone.

Evaluation uses RULER and PaperTrail, a long-context scientific reading benchmark the authors built. At 10M tokens, one D-LSA attention layer prefills 22.7× and decodes 4.6× faster than sparse attention on GLM-5.3-Flash, and 72.4× and 42.5× faster than full attention on Qwen-3.8-27B, with similar accuracy. N-LSA matches full-attention accuracy with a 1.6× per-layer training speedup at 128k tokens.

Limitations: the KV cache still grows linearly with context, tree search loses accuracy faster than flat search past 1M tokens on GLM-5.3-Flash, and N-LSA was tested only at about 0.5B parameters with flat search.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Sparse attention indexers that score every key dominate cost at ultra-long context, so LSA clusters keys instead.

digest_headlines.heading: Sparse Attention
digest_headlines.headline: At 10M tokens the indexer takes 98% of sparse attention's prefill time, and current indexers still scan every key.

digest_headlines.heading: Latent Sparse Attention (LSA)
digest_headlines.headline: LSA clusters keys in a learned latent space, and each query scores only bucket centroids, flat or as a tree.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: D-LSA keeps accuracy close to baselines up to 10M tokens, and N-LSA matches full-attention validation loss at 128k.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Tree search loses accuracy faster than flat past 1M tokens, and native training was tested only at small scale.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: LSA offers a practical route to ultra-long context attention, through distillation of pre-trained models or native training.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers oracle key-budget tests, method symbols, training data, PaperTrail, evaluation setup, and parallelism details.
